source.text: Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν, ὁ μὴ εἰσερχόμενος διὰ τῆς θύρας εἰς τὴν αὐλὴν τῶν προβάτων ἀλλὰ ἀναβαίνων ἀλλαχόθεν ἐκεῖνος κλέπτης ἐστὶν καὶ λῃστής·

records.literal_gloss: "Truly truly I say to you, the [one] not entering through the door into the fold of the sheep but going up from elsewhere, that one a thief is and a bandit;

en.L: "Truly, truly I say to you, the one who does not enter through the door into the fold of the sheep, but climbs up from elsewhere, that one is a thief and a bandit.
en.B: "Truly, truly, I tell you, anyone who does not go into the sheepfold by the door, but climbs in from somewhere else, is a thief and a bandit.
en.R: "I tell you the truth: anyone who does not go into the sheep pen through the door, but climbs over the wall somewhere else, is a thief and a bandit.

decisions.choice: the speech goes straight on from 9:41: "you" are the Pharisees of 9:40-41
alternatives: a new speech to a new audience
decisions.reason: There is no change of place, time or listeners between 9:41 and 10:1; the chapter division is later than the text. Jesus has just told the Pharisees who claim to see that their sin remains (9:41), and he goes on speaking to them (10:6 says he spoke "to them"). The picture of the shepherd and the thieves follows directly on their treatment of the man who was healed and thrown out (9:34).

decisions.choice: the fold: a walled enclosure for sheep with a single entrance
alternatives: the courtyard of a house only
decisions.reason: The word means an enclosed yard. Sheepfolds were enclosures with walls of stone, often topped with thorns, and one opening; sometimes the yard of a house served. The sheep were kept there at night. Anyone who came in over the wall instead of through the entrance had no right to be there. The same word is used for the courtyard of the high priest (18:15).

decisions.choice: thief: one who steals by stealth; bandit: one who robs by violence
alternatives: two words for the same person with no difference
decisions.reason: The two words are not the same. The first is the ordinary word for a thief, used of Judas (12:6). The second is a robber who uses force, the kind who attacked travelers on the road (Luke 10:30); it is also the word for Barabbas (18:40), and in the first century it was used of armed rebels. Together they describe someone who takes what is not his, by cunning or by force.

decisions.choice: the shepherd picture draws on Ezekiel 34, Jeremiah 23:1-4 and Psalm 23
decisions.reason: The Scriptures often call Israel God's flock and its leaders shepherds. Ezekiel 34 condemns the shepherds of Israel who fed themselves and scattered the sheep, and promises that God himself will seek his sheep and set one shepherd, his servant David, over them (Ezekiel 34:11-16, 23). Jeremiah 23:1-4 pronounces woe on shepherds who destroy and scatter the flock. Psalm 23 calls God the shepherd who leads his sheep to pasture. That the thieves and bandits here are meant as the false shepherds of Ezekiel 34, in the persons of the Pharisees who threw the man out (9:34), is likely from the setting but not stated; the verbal links are clearer in 10:11-16.

decisions.choice: Truly, truly I say to you (L); Truly, truly, I tell you (B); I tell you the truth (R)
decisions.reason: The book-wide rendering for John (see 1:51), recorded once in this passage; it covers 10:7 as well.

decisions.choice: the fold of the sheep (L); the sheepfold (B); the sheep pen (R); a thief and a bandit at every level
decisions.reason: "Bandit" keeps the two Greek words distinct (meaning decision m3) and is used again in 10:8. "Door" is kept at every level so that "I am the door" (10:7, 9) is heard as the same word.

decisions.choice: climbs over the wall somewhere else
decisions.reason: Readable says plainly what climbing in "from elsewhere" means in a walled fold (meaning decision m2).

source.text: ὁ δὲ εἰσερχόμενος διὰ τῆς θύρας ποιμήν ἐστιν τῶν προβάτων.

records.literal_gloss: The [one] but entering through the door shepherd is of the sheep.

en.L: But the one who enters through the door is [the] shepherd of the sheep.
en.B: But the one who goes in through the door is the shepherd of the sheep.
en.R: But the one who goes in through the door is the shepherd of the sheep.

decisions.choice: shepherd without the article: he is the one with a right to the sheep, the shepherd as opposed to a thief
alternatives: the one Good Shepherd already named
decisions.reason: The Greek has no article with "shepherd". The point is the contrast with verse 1: whoever comes by the door shows himself a shepherd, not a thief. At this stage of the picture the shepherd is not yet identified; Jesus names himself the good shepherd in 10:11.

decisions.choice: entering through the door: coming openly by the rightful way
alternatives: a reference to Jesus as the door (10:7)
decisions.reason: In the picture the door is simply the proper entrance, opened for the shepherd by the doorkeeper (verse 3). Only in 10:7 does Jesus apply the door to himself, in a second step of the picture.

decisions.choice: [the] shepherd
decisions.reason: Literal brackets the article English needs (meaning decision m1).

source.text: τούτῳ ὁ θυρωρὸς ἀνοίγει, καὶ τὰ πρόβατα τῆς φωνῆς αὐτοῦ ἀκούει καὶ τὰ ἴδια πρόβατα φωνεῖ κατ’ ὄνομα καὶ ἐξάγει αὐτά.

records.literal_gloss: To this [one] the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep the voice of him hear, and the own sheep he calls by name and leads out them.

en.L: For this one the doorkeeper opens, and the sheep hear his voice, and he calls his own sheep by name and leads them out.
en.B: For him the doorkeeper opens the door, and the sheep hear his voice. He calls each of his own sheep by name and leads them out.
en.R: The one who keeps watch at the door opens it for him, and the sheep listen to his voice. He calls each of his own sheep by name and leads them out.

decisions.choice: the doorkeeper: a watchman who guarded the entrance of the fold
alternatives: a figure for some particular person
decisions.reason: Where several flocks shared one fold for the night, a watchman kept the entrance and opened it in the morning to the shepherds he knew. The doorkeeper is part of the scene and is not explained in the passage; nothing in the text says whom he stands for.

decisions.choice: his own sheep: his flock among others in the same fold
alternatives: all the sheep in the fold
decisions.reason: The phrase "his own" sets his sheep apart from others kept in the fold. He calls each of his own by name, and those are the ones he leads out (10:14, 27).

decisions.choice: hear his voice: listen and respond to him
decisions.reason: Hearing a voice in John is responding to the one who speaks (5:25; 10:16, 27; 18:37). The sheep know whose voice it is and answer it.

decisions.choice: leads out: perhaps an echo of God leading his people out of Egypt and of Numbers 27:17
alternatives: an ordinary word for taking sheep out to pasture, with no echo
decisions.reason: The verb is the ordinary one for leading out. In the Greek Old Testament it is used of God bringing Israel out of Egypt (Exodus 20:2) and in Moses's prayer for a leader who will lead the people out and bring them in, so that they are not like sheep without a shepherd (Numbers 27:16-17). Whether John intends the echo here is uncertain.

decisions.choice: his, he, him for the shepherd in 10:1-5 written without a deity_pronoun span; pronouns for Jesus from 10:6 on take one
alternatives: capitalisable pronouns for the shepherd in the picture
decisions.reason: In 10:1-5 Jesus tells a picture (10:6), and the shepherd is a figure in it, like the bridegroom of 3:29; his pronouns are not pronouns for God or Christ. When Jesus applies the picture to himself from 10:7 ("I am the door"), and when the narrator speaks of him (10:6), the pronouns for Jesus take the usual span.

decisions.choice: opens the door (B); opens it (R); calls each of his own sheep by name (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable say what is opened; Readable also describes the doorkeeper's work instead of using the title. "Each" brings out that the Greek phrase means name by name.

source.text: ὅταν τὰ ἴδια πάντα ἐκβάλῃ, ἔμπροσθεν αὐτῶν πορεύεται, καὶ τὰ πρόβατα αὐτῷ ἀκολουθεῖ, ὅτι οἴδασιν τὴν φωνὴν αὐτοῦ·

records.literal_gloss: When the own all he puts out, ahead of them he goes, and the sheep him follow, because they know the voice of him;

en.L: When he has put out all his own, he goes ahead of them, and the sheep follow him, because they know his voice.
en.B: Once he has brought all his own sheep out, he walks on ahead, and the sheep follow him because they know his voice.
en.R: When all his own sheep are out, he walks in front of them. The sheep follow him, because they know his voice.

decisions.choice: put out: bring out, with the sense of getting every one of them out
decisions.reason: The verb often means to throw or drive out, and it is the word used in 9:34-35 when the Pharisees threw the healed man out. Here the shepherd puts his own sheep out of the fold; what the authorities did to the man in hostility, the shepherd does for his flock's good. The force here is not violence but making sure that all his own are out.

decisions.choice: the shepherd walks in front and the sheep follow
alternatives: the shepherd drives the flock from behind
decisions.reason: Shepherds in the land of Israel led their flocks from the front, calling to them, and the sheep followed the voice they knew. The picture of a shepherd going before his flock is used of God (Psalm 80:1; Isaiah 40:11).

decisions.choice: because they know his voice: knowing his voice is the reason they follow
decisions.reason: The sheep do not follow because they are forced but because they recognise the one who calls them, which prepares for 10:14 ("I know my own and my own know me").

decisions.choice: all his own sheep; brought ... out (B, R)
decisions.reason: The Greek says "all his own"; Balanced and Readable supply "sheep", which the context makes clear, and use the gentler "brought out" for the verb (meaning decision m1).

source.text: ἀλλοτρίῳ δὲ οὐ μὴ ἀκολουθήσουσιν ἀλλὰ φεύξονται ἀπ’ αὐτοῦ, ὅτι οὐκ οἴδασι τῶν ἀλλοτρίων τὴν φωνήν.

records.literal_gloss: A stranger but not not they will follow but they will flee from him, because not they know of the strangers the voice.

en.L: But a stranger they will by no means follow, but they will flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers.
en.B: They will not follow a stranger at all. They will run from him, because they do not know the voices of strangers.
en.R: But they will never go after a stranger. They will run away from him, because they do not know a stranger's voice.

decisions.choice: a strong denial: they will certainly not follow
alternatives: a simple future: they will not follow
decisions.reason: The Greek puts two negatives together, the strongest way to deny something in the future.

decisions.choice: stranger: someone who does not belong to them
decisions.reason: The word means someone who belongs to another, not to this flock. It is not a foreigner by nation but a voice the sheep do not recognise as their shepherd's.

decisions.choice: the picture fits the man in chapter 9: he would not follow the Pharisees but listened to Jesus
alternatives: no connection with the preceding story
decisions.reason: The man born blind refused to be led by the Pharisees who questioned him (9:27-33), was thrown out (9:34), and then heard Jesus and worshiped him (9:35-38). The picture describes what has just happened, though Jesus does not name him.

decisions.choice: not ... at all (B); never (R); run (away)
decisions.reason: Plain words for the strong denial (meaning decision m1) and for fleeing.

source.text: ταύτην τὴν παροιμίαν εἶπεν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· ἐκεῖνοι δὲ οὐκ ἔγνωσαν τίνα ἦν ἃ ἐλάλει αὐτοῖς.

records.literal_gloss: This the figure said to them the Jesus; those but not understood what were [the things] which he was speaking to them.

en.L: Jesus told them this figure of speech, but they did not understand what the things were that {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} was saying to them.
en.B: Jesus spoke this figure of speech to them, but they did not grasp what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} meant by it.
en.R: Jesus used this picture to teach them, but they did not understand what {{deity_pronoun:he|He}} meant.

decisions.choice: a figure of speech: a saying with a hidden meaning that has to be worked out
alternatives: a parable in the sense of the stories in the other Gospels
decisions.reason: This is not the word the other Gospels use for Jesus's parables. It means a veiled or figurative saying, and in the Greek Old Testament it is used for proverbs. John uses it again when Jesus promises that he will no longer speak in figures but plainly (16:25, 29). Here it describes the picture of 10:1-5, whose meaning Jesus has not yet given.

decisions.choice: them: the Pharisees of 9:40-41
decisions.reason: The emphatic "those" points back to the people Jesus has been speaking to, the Pharisees who said, "We are not blind too, are we?" (9:40). Those who claim to see do not understand.

decisions.choice: they did not understand what his words meant
alternatives: they did not hear what he said
decisions.reason: They heard the words but did not grasp what they referred to, as often in John (8:27; 12:16). This is why Jesus goes on to explain (10:7).

decisions.choice: figure of speech (L, B); picture (R)
decisions.reason: "Parable" would bring in the word of the other Gospels, which John does not use (meaning decision m1). Readable uses a plain word for the same thing.

decisions.choice: Jesus told them (L); Jesus spoke ... to them (B)
alternatives: This figure of speech Jesus told them
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "this figure" first for emphasis; English puts the subject first, and Literal follows English order here because the fronted object reads awkwardly.

source.text: Εἶπεν οὖν πάλιν αὐτοῖς ὁ Ἰησοῦς· Ἀμὴν ἀμὴν λέγω ὑμῖν ὅτι ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα τῶν προβάτων.

records.literal_gloss: Said therefore again to them the Jesus, "Truly truly I say to you that I am the door of the sheep.

en.L: So Jesus said again to them, "Truly, truly I say to you, I am the door of the sheep.
en.B: So Jesus spoke to them again: "Truly, truly, I tell you, I am the door for the sheep.
en.R: So Jesus spoke to them again. "I tell you the truth: I am the door for the sheep.

decisions.choice: the door of the sheep (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the shepherd of the sheep (one early papyrus, P75, and some Coptic witnesses)
decisions.reason: Almost all manuscripts read "the door". A few early witnesses, the papyrus P75 among them, read "the shepherd", which is probably a change to fit 10:11. "The door" is the harder reading and is supported by 10:9. A footnote gives the other reading. A reviewer should check this against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: the door for the sheep: the door by which the sheep go in and out
alternatives: the door to the sheep, by which shepherds come to them
decisions.reason: In verses 1-2 the door is the way the shepherd comes to the sheep; in verse 9 it is the way the sheep go in and out. Jesus is the second here, as verse 9 makes plain, but the first is not excluded: those who came another way (verse 8) did not come through him.

decisions.choice: I am with a predicate: one of the sayings in which Jesus says who he is
alternatives: an echo of the divine name
decisions.reason: With a predicate the words are ordinary grammar. It is one of a series of such sayings (6:35; 8:12; 10:9, 11; 11:25; 14:6; 15:1), in which Jesus takes a picture and says that he is what it points to.

decisions.choice: so ... again: because they did not understand, he speaks again and explains
decisions.reason: The connecting word ties this to 10:6: Jesus explains the figure, taking up its parts one by one, first the door and then (10:11) the shepherd.

decisions.choice: the door of the sheep (L); the door for the sheep (B, R)
decisions.reason: Balanced and Readable show which door is meant (meaning decision m2). "Door" is kept at every level, as in 10:1-2.

source.text: πάντες ὅσοι ἦλθον πρὸ ἐμοῦ κλέπται εἰσὶν καὶ λῃσταί· ἀλλ’ οὐκ ἤκουσαν αὐτῶν τὰ πρόβατα.

records.literal_gloss: All as many as came before me thieves are and bandits; but not heard them the sheep.

en.L: All who came before {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} are thieves and bandits; but the sheep did not hear them.
en.B: All who came before {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}} are thieves and bandits, but the sheep did not give them a hearing.
en.R: All who came before {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, claiming to be shepherds, are thieves and bandits. But the sheep did not listen to them.

decisions.choice: all who came before me: those who came claiming to lead God's people in his place, not Moses and the prophets
alternatives: every teacher and prophet before Jesus
only the Pharisees of his own day
decisions.reason: Jesus speaks of the prophets with respect: Moses wrote about him (5:46), Abraham rejoiced to see his day (8:56), and Isaiah saw his glory (12:41). The ones meant are those who came to the flock by another way, as in verse 1: leaders who used the people for themselves, like the shepherds of Ezekiel 34, and men who claimed to be the deliverer and led people into ruin. The present tense "are" may point especially to leaders still at work, such as those who had just thrown out the healed man. Who exactly is meant is not stated.

decisions.choice: before me (SBLGNT)
alternatives: the words left out (some early manuscripts)
decisions.reason: Some early witnesses leave out "before me", probably to avoid the impression that Jesus condemned the prophets; without them the sentence reads "All who came are thieves and bandits". The SBLGNT keeps the words. A reviewer should check the evidence against the apparatus.

decisions.choice: did not hear them: did not listen to them or follow them
alternatives: did not hear the sound of their voices
decisions.reason: As in verse 3, hearing means responding. The true sheep did not follow them, as the sheep in verse 5 flee from a stranger.

decisions.choice: claiming to be shepherds
decisions.reason: Readable makes explicit who "came": not everyone who lived earlier, but those who came to the flock as leaders (meaning decision m1). This goes beyond what the Greek says and reflects the uncertain decision m1.

decisions.choice: before {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}
decisions.reason: From here Jesus applies the picture to himself, so "me" takes the deity_pronoun span (see 10:3).

source.text: ἐγώ εἰμι ἡ θύρα· δι’ ἐμοῦ ἐάν τις εἰσέλθῃ σωθήσεται καὶ εἰσελεύσεται καὶ ἐξελεύσεται καὶ νομὴν εὑρήσει.

records.literal_gloss: I am the door; through me if anyone enters he will be saved and will go in and will go out and pasture will find.

en.L: I am the door; through {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, if anyone enters, {{gender:they|he}} will be saved, and will go in and will go out and will find pasture.
en.B: I am the door. If anyone goes in through {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{gender:they|he}} will be saved, going in and going out and finding pasture.
en.R: I am the door. If anyone comes in through {{deity_pronoun:me|Me}}, {{gender:they|he}} will be saved. {{gender:They|He}} will go in and out, and will find good grass to eat.

decisions.choice: will be saved: kept safe and given life, as a sheep in the fold and as a person who comes to Jesus
decisions.reason: In the picture the sheep that comes in by the door is safe from thieves. Applied to people, being saved in John means being rescued from perishing and given eternal life (3:16-17; 5:34; 12:47). Both are in view.

decisions.choice: go in and go out: live freely and safely
decisions.reason: Going in and going out is a Hebrew way of speaking of the whole of a person's life and daily movement (Deuteronomy 28:6; Psalm 121:8). Moses asked for a leader who would go out and come in before the people, so that they would not be like sheep without a shepherd (Numbers 27:17).

decisions.choice: find pasture: the shepherd's provision, as in Psalm 23 and Ezekiel 34
decisions.reason: God leads his flock to green pastures (Psalm 23:2) and promises to feed his sheep in good pasture on the mountains of Israel (Ezekiel 34:14).

decisions.choice: through me: placed first for emphasis
decisions.reason: The Greek puts "through me" before "if anyone enters": it is through him, and no other way (verse 1), that anyone comes in.

decisions.choice: anyone ... {{gender:they|he}}
decisions.reason: "Anyone" means any person, man or woman; the following pronoun takes the gender setting, with "he" as the alternative.

decisions.choice: good grass to eat
decisions.reason: Readable says what pasture is for sheep, a place to graze.

source.text: ὁ κλέπτης οὐκ ἔρχεται εἰ μὴ ἵνα κλέψῃ καὶ θύσῃ καὶ ἀπολέσῃ· ἐγὼ ἦλθον ἵνα ζωὴν ἔχωσιν καὶ περισσὸν ἔχωσιν.

records.literal_gloss: The thief not comes except that he may steal and slaughter and destroy; I came that life they may have and abundance they may have.

en.L: The thief does not come except to steal and slaughter and destroy; I came that they may have life and may have [it] beyond measure.
en.B: The thief comes for no other reason than to steal and slaughter and destroy. I came so that they may have life, and have it in overflowing measure.
en.R: A thief has only one reason for coming: to steal the sheep, kill them and destroy them. But I came so that they can have life, life that overflows.

decisions.choice: slaughter: kill as an animal is killed for its meat
decisions.reason: The verb is used of killing animals, often in sacrifice, and of slaughtering for food (Luke 15:23). In a picture of sheep the sense is butchering; there is no thought of sacrifice here.

decisions.choice: destroy and life: perishing and eternal life
alternatives: physical harm and physical life only
decisions.reason: The verb "destroy" is the one John uses for perishing (3:16; 10:28), and the life Jesus gives is eternal life, which begins now (3:15-16; 5:24; 10:28). The thief brings the sheep to ruin; Jesus came to give them life that does not end.

decisions.choice: more than enough: life in full measure, beyond what is needed
decisions.reason: The word means what goes beyond the measure, an overflowing amount. It describes the fullness of the life Jesus gives, not wealth or comfort. The contrast is with shepherds who fed themselves instead of the flock (Ezekiel 34:2-3).

decisions.choice: the thief comes only to ...; I came that ...: two comings set against each other
decisions.reason: The construction "not ... except" limits the thief's purpose to harm. Jesus's "I came" answers it and recalls "all who came before me" (verse 8).

decisions.choice: beyond measure (L); in overflowing measure (B); life that overflows (R)
decisions.reason: These words say what the Greek word says, an amount that goes past the measure (meaning decision m3), without the wording familiar from other versions. Literal brackets "it", which the Greek leaves understood.

decisions.choice: to steal the sheep, kill them and destroy them
alternatives: to steal and kill and destroy
decisions.reason: Readable supplies the sheep as the object, which the picture implies.
